essays_that_worked.author: David M.
essays_that_worked.title: The Secret Ingredient is Connection
essays_that_worked.about: Baking for a team, and ditching recipes to invent original desserts, shows how the writer experiments, builds community, and brings people from different backgrounds together.

essays_that_worked.author: Etina R.
essays_that_worked.title: Developing Roots
essays_that_worked.about: The writer's passion for trees becomes a metaphor for weathering hardship, finding where they belong, and weighing self-reliance against mutual support.

essays_that_worked.author: Gillian H.
essays_that_worked.title: The Two Sides of America
essays_that_worked.about: Contrasts city life in Chicago with summers doing farm work alongside family in rural Mississippi, and what living in both worlds taught the writer about people and hard work.

essays_that_worked.author: Ruoni T.
essays_that_worked.title: Clean Closet
essays_that_worked.about: Finally emptying a closet crammed with childhood keepsakes leads the writer to think about nostalgia, letting go, and opening up to new people and experiences.

essays_that_worked.author: Ruoyu X.
essays_that_worked.title: In the Belly of the Ship
essays_that_worked.about: Recalls a tough internship at sea on a cargo vessel, where hard physical routines and a tight-knit crew taught the writer to keep going after failures.

essays_that_worked.author: Tymofii “Tima” Kolisnyk
essays_that_worked.about: Framed as old digital files resurfacing on a far-future birthday, it traces leaving wartime Ukraine, schooling abroad, and the people and pastimes that rebuilt the writer's sense of home.

essays_that_worked.author: Taylor Barnes
essays_that_worked.about: Describes a Girl Scout troop's years-long grassroots campaign to change the wording of the Girl Scout Promise, its defeat in a national vote, and what advocacy taught the writer.

essays_that_worked.author: Benjamin Frenkel
essays_that_worked.about: Imagines the forces running the writer's life as a panel of powerful advisers, and realizing that leaning on rigid structure had limits and it was time to take charge.

essays_that_worked.author: Shiwani Paudel
essays_that_worked.about: A summer-camp moment of not matching a famous book character leads into reflections on frequent family moves, fitting in, and finding community through service.

essays_that_worked.author: Nina De Jesus Santiago
essays_that_worked.about: Uses a puppet-and-strings metaphor for breaking free of family expectations after their parents' divorce and finding purpose through history and volunteering, including translating for immigrants.

essays_that_worked.author: Rowan Johnson
essays_that_worked.about: A tense moment with a difficult horse at a show reshapes the writer's approach to training and care, and that new patience carries over into relationships at home.

essays_that_worked.author: Emily Huryk
essays_that_worked.about: A hospital worker who is not religious describes praying with a patient, reflecting on offering comfort and meeting people where they are across differences in belief.

essays_that_worked.author: Martin Amuso
essays_that_worked.about: Describes a Crohn's disease diagnosis, turning to Wiffle Ball as an escape while ill, and regaining strength and gratitude once treatment finally began.

essays_that_worked.author: Phoebe Hughes
essays_that_worked.title: Telling us about yourself through your relationships with others
essays_that_worked.about: Explores how an older sister, and the different women the sister brought into the family's life, shaped the writer's identity, empathy, and feminism.

essays_that_worked.author: Elizabeth Madden
essays_that_worked.title: Using what you’ve learned to make a change in your life
essays_that_worked.about: Links family hikes in Acadia National Park to a news story about youth climate activists that pushed the writer toward environmental clubs, coursework, and sustainable habits.

essays_that_worked.author: Nancy Owusu
essays_that_worked.title: Learning to appreciate your family responsibilities
essays_that_worked.about: Reflects on the constant household duties the writer was asked to take on, and coming to see them as their parents' way of teaching balance and hard work.

essays_that_worked.author: Anonymous
essays_that_worked.title: Standing up for your beliefs
essays_that_worked.about: Draws on the careers of the women in the writer's family and a charged classroom debate to show a drive toward law, advocacy, and women's rights.

essays_that_worked.author: Jackson Spallone
essays_that_worked.title: Finding a life lesson in a hobby
essays_that_worked.about: After a shoulder injury halts lacrosse, the writer takes up gardening and hydroponics, and describes how tending plants built patience that carried into school and the return to sport.

essays_that_worked.author: Nikeya Tankard
essays_that_worked.title: Considering a physical feature and its role in your identity
essays_that_worked.about: Examines the recurring choice between wearing curly or straightened hair and what that duality means for the writer's heritage and sense of self.

essays_that_worked.author: Elle Yarborough
essays_that_worked.title: Cooking conjures up a worldview
essays_that_worked.about: Making an oversized pancake with a friend opens a reflection on cooking as the writer's main way of showing care for the people closest to them.

essays_that_worked.author: Riley Anderson
essays_that_worked.title: Being an outsider doesn’t mean not belonging
essays_that_worked.about: Describes playing golf as the lone girl among teenage boys and without country-club access, and finding belonging in the sport anyway.

essays_that_worked.author: Shaan Merchant
essays_that_worked.about: Rowdy family word games and relatives speaking different languages anchor a reflection on the writer's love of words, communication, food, and comedy.

essays_that_worked.author: Ray Parker
essays_that_worked.about: Describes growing up in a home packed with scientific equipment, raised by parents who blend science and art, and how that shaped the writer's curiosity.

essays_that_worked.author: Evana Wilson
essays_that_worked.about: Describes hunting for a quiet place to do homework in a small, crowded, noisy family home and finding an unlikely hideaway.

essays_that_worked.author: Celeste Teng
essays_that_worked.about: Explains why Tufts' interdisciplinary literary and visual studies major appeals to a student from Singapore who wants to study film and literature across cultures.

essays_that_worked.prompt_answered: Celebrate the Role of Sports in Your Life
essays_that_worked.author: Tessa Garces
essays_that_worked.about: Traces a path from reluctant young swimmer to committed competitor, and how habits from the pool shape the way the writer approaches life.

essays_that_worked.title: My Pillows & Me
essays_that_worked.about: Uses a collection of bed pillows, each tied to a different interest or trait, to sketch the many sides of the writer's personality.

essays_that_worked.title: Laptop Stickers
essays_that_worked.about: Walks through the stickers on the writer's laptop as symbols of their passions, communities, and experiences.

essays_that_worked.title: Deli Connections
essays_that_worked.about: Describes how a job at a neighborhood deli fed the writer's language learning, global interests, and sense of community.

essays_that_worked.title: Travel and Language
essays_that_worked.about: Traces a love of travel to learning several languages and the personal connections those languages make possible.

essays_that_worked.title: What Rocks Tell Us
essays_that_worked.about: Uses a rock collection as a through-line to reflect on creativity, resilience, and personal growth.

essays_that_worked.title: Five Families
essays_that_worked.about: Recounts living with five different host families during an exchange program and what adapting to each household taught the writer.

essays_that_worked.prompt_answered: What is your impression of Duke as a university and community, and why do you believe it is a good match for your goals, values, and interests? If there is something specific that attracts you to our academic offerings in Trinity College of Arts and Sciences or the Pratt School of Engineering, or to our co-curricular opportunities, feel free to include that too.
essays_that_worked.about: A why-Duke answer connecting a goal of using robotics on environmental problems to a mechanical engineering major, an energy and environment certificate, specific courses, and faculty research.

essays_that_worked.prompt_answered: Write a short thank-you note to someone you have not yet thanked and would like to acknowledge. (We encourage you to share this note with that person, if possible, and reflect on the experience!)
essays_that_worked.author: Juju
essays_that_worked.about: A thank-you letter to a teacher who made a male-dominated programming class feel welcoming, giving the writer confidence to take on an ambitious creative coding project.

essays_that_worked.prompt_answered: What field of study appeals to you the most right now? (Note: Applicants select from a drop-down list.) Reflect on what has led you to this interest.
essays_that_worked.about: Explains how break-ins at a family business and a relative's influence sparked the writer's interest in using technology to improve security.

essays_that_worked.prompt_answered: How did you manage a situation or challenge that you didn’t expect? What did you learn from it?
essays_that_worked.about: An injured baseball player describes moving from playing to helping run the team through data analysis and strategy advice during a playoff run.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer follows one thread, a love of stories, from books heard as a small child through audio and screen media to the comedic writing and audio shows they now produce. They then present studying film and media at Yale as a natural continuation of it.
structure: Opens by naming the one interest that ties everything together
Moves quickly from childhood reading to audio and visual media
Lands on the creative projects the writer runs today
Frames the intended major as the next step, with possible directions
why_it_works: One clear theme lets a 100-word answer feel complete instead of rushed.
A quick timeline shows the interest grew over years, not overnight.
Finish by linking what you already make to what you want to study.
sample_essays.match_note: Written when this Yale prompt had a shorter word limit.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer answers with one invented course. A playful, attention-grabbing title comes first, then a subtitle that shows the class would be a serious history of misleading news in the U.S. and the damage it has done.
structure: Leads with a funny, memorable course title
Uses a colon to pivot from the joke to the substance
Subtitle names the real topic and how broad the course is
why_it_works: A title that makes readers smile, then a subtitle that proves the class is rigorous.
The chosen topic hints at what the writer cares about without stating it.
With a tiny limit, one sharp line can do the work of a paragraph.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes staying up late building a fan-made video game with an online team while covering several roles. They single out a small nightly ritual, posting progress before bed and waking up to teammates' replies, as the thing that keeps them going.
structure: Opens with a quick run of the jobs they handle
Zooms into a specific late-night work routine
Highlights one small, rewarding moment with teammates
Ends on why they keep coming back to the project
why_it_works: A side project missing from the activities list reveals a new side of you.
One concrete ritual says more about drive than naming the trait.
Mentioning teammates hints at collaboration without spelling it out.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer recounts a summer lab experiment tracking how polymer samples changed and how it was paired with a research partner's work on nanoscale filters. They close by pointing to how the combined work could improve water filtration and make clean water easier to reach.
structure: Opens with a dated, action-first statement of the experiment
Briefly explains the method in plain terms
Links the work to a research partner's project
Widens to a real-world use: cleaner water
why_it_works: Explaining the method in a line proves you understand the science.
Ending on real-world use answers why the research matters.
Pick something the rest of your application can't show in detail.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Troubled that their school's mascot carried a racist history, the writer posted publicly in favor of changing it. Amid hostile replies, they messaged one critic privately, and the two swapped sources for days. The writer reflects on what made that exchange work and how they would create more spaces for respectful disagreement.
structure: Opens with the stakes: an honor tied to a contested mascot
Shows the public post and the backlash it drew
Shifts to a private, days-long exchange with one critic
Both sides dig into each other's sources and rethink
Closes with lessons and a plan for future dialogue
why_it_works: Moving from a public fight to a one-on-one talk shows maturity.
Treating the other side's evidence seriously makes your reflection believable.
End with what you will do differently, not only what you felt.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: A political cartoon in a language class sets off an argument that turns personal and leaves classmates avoiding one another. Looking back, the writer sees that people were pushing views instead of explaining them, admits to having quietly picked a side, and resolves to hear everyone out before judging.
structure: Opens in the classroom as the cartoon sparks debate
Shows the argument sliding into insults
Describes the lasting rift among classmates
Reflects, admits personal bias, and commits to listening first
why_it_works: A group conflict works when you examine your own part in it.
Admitting your bias makes the lesson feel earned, not preachy.
Showing the aftermath proves the disagreement mattered beyond one class.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes working at a community farm: digging crops, sorting crates and, starting on a rainy first day, taking charge of packing the delivery truck more efficiently. They explain they return for the people and the gratitude around the food, and reflect on what a group achieves that no one person could.
structure: Opens by stating the role and listing hands-on tasks
Narrows to one job the writer owns: loading the truck
Shows a small fix that improved deliveries
Explains what keeps the writer coming back
Ends with a reflection on shared effort
why_it_works: Naming your specific job shows contribution, not just membership.
Physical, sensory details make an unusual community easy to picture.
Answer the why-it-matters part directly before you close.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with a parent's offhand reaction to a video they made for a local LGBT center about workplace discrimination against queer Chinese employees. Backing up to show how the video was made and the parent's earlier disapproval, they reflect on how the work made a community feel human and why diversity matters to them.
structure: Opens with a parent's spoken reaction that signals a change
Backs up to explain how the video was made
Reveals the parent's earlier disapproval to raise the stakes
Reflects on what the moment showed about the work's impact
Closes with a brief statement of values
why_it_works: Starting with a reaction, then explaining it, builds curiosity.
One person's change of heart shows impact more vividly than view counts.
Specific production choices prove the writer did the work.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer moves from a light opening about food to their Jewish heritage and relatives lost in the Holocaust. They describe joining a Holocaust center's student board, holding weekly discussions and helping build a website about one survivor, and close hoping to find peers who share their commitments as well as people unlike them.
structure: Opens with a playful line before turning serious
Connects family history to a sense of responsibility
Shows concrete action: the board role and survivor website
Ends with hopes for community at college
why_it_works: A light opening can ease into a heavy topic without feeling abrupt.
Pair an identity with the actions you have taken because of it.
Say how you would keep the work going on campus; this sample only hints at it.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: After a lighthearted opening about food, the writer turns to their Jewish heritage and relatives lost in the Holocaust, then shows what they did about it: serving on a Holocaust center's student board, joining weekly talks on present-day oppression and helping build a website about a survivor. They end hoping to find both kindred and different peers.
structure: Opens with a playful line, then turns serious
Links family history to a sense of duty
Shows specific action on a student board
Ends with what the writer seeks in a college community
why_it_works: Show what your background led you to do, not only who you are.
Keep to one identity and one project to fit Harvard's short limit.
Add a sentence on what you would bring to Harvard specifically.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer challenges the assumption that an Asian American affinity group must be uniform, pointing to members of different grades, genders and home countries alongside shared moments like embarrassment over lunches from home. They reflect that people who look alike can differ while different people share a lot, and aim to learn from both.
structure: Opens by questioning an assumption about the group
Shows variety within the group through specific details
Adds a shared, relatable experience members have in common
Reflects on what diversity means and states a goal
why_it_works: Challenging a common assumption gives a familiar topic a fresh angle.
Small shared details make a group feel real.
Turn your reflection into a goal for how you will contribute.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes a running disagreement with their father over pandemic mask rules, then faces a choice when invited on a family trip full of activities they both enjoy. They decide to go, but only on clear conditions, keeping the relationship while holding firm on public-health limits.
structure: Opens by stating the disagreement and both positions
Introduces a tempting invitation that creates a dilemma
Explains the decision to go with set conditions
Ends on a light image tied to the writer's values
why_it_works: Lay out both positions in a sentence or two so the conflict is clear fast.
A real dilemma shows how you weigh competing values.
Show the action you took and its limits, not only your feelings.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer explains they argue most with a grandfather raised in India, then zooms in on a running debate about headache remedies: store-bought pills versus balms and oils. Through it they learn to word objections gently, keep logic separate from hurt feelings, and see a good argument as an exchange instead of a contest.
structure: Opens by naming the person and why their views differ
Uses one small, recurring debate as the example
Gives both sides' reasoning fairly
Shows a concrete change in how the writer phrases things
Ends with a broader view of what arguments are for
why_it_works: Giving the other person's reasoning fairly shows you actually listened.
A specific new habit of speech proves the lesson stuck.
Different backgrounds can explain a disagreement without blaming anyone.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with a comedy film's celebration of always agreeing, then shows how policy debate trained them to research both sides, question tidy answers and spot flawed reasoning, even in advertising. They close by explaining that they now hold off on agreeing until they have weighed other views, circling back to the film.
structure: Opens with a film reference that sets up a contrast
Notes the risk of agreeing without questioning
Shows how debate built a habit of skepticism
Returns to the film to close the loop
why_it_works: Frame an activity by the habit of mind it built, not its awards.
A pop-culture hook works when it sets up your actual point.
One everyday example, like reading ads, shows the skill outside the activity.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens mid-workout, running stairs and hearing their own breathing, then reveals it is a ballet school's conditioning class. They make the case that dancers are athletes by describing demanding moves and drills, and close by contrasting how hard their first class felt with how natural leaps and turns feel now.
structure: Opens in a physical moment that hides the activity
Reveals ballet and pushes back on a stereotype
Lists demanding skills to prove the point
Ends by contrasting the first class with today
why_it_works: Delaying the reveal makes a familiar activity surprising.
Technical details show expertise without bragging.
A then-versus-now ending shows growth in one sentence.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with a rapid list of political issues they follow, ties them to an immigrant family background and a chosen international relations focus, then describes favorite classes, independent research on parliamentary systems, a professor to learn from and study abroad. They finish by applying the degree to local issues and a career in global affairs.
structure: Opens with a quick list of issues the writer cares about
Links those issues to family background and program choice
Shows academic groundwork: classes, research and a professor
Applies the degree to local community problems
Ends with a long-term career goal
why_it_works: Show what you would do with the degree at home, not just abroad.
Past research proves the future plan has roots.
Harvard allows far fewer words, so keep only the clearest one or two goals.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with a striking image linking the brain to the stars, then recounts a months-long search for a diagnosis at age 14. Grateful their own condition is manageable, they show how classes, a neuroscience program and a lecture on health gaps abroad shaped a plan for pediatric neurology and humanitarian work.
structure: Opens with a vivid image and a turn to personal illness
Shifts focus from personal luck to others' needs
Shows how classes and a lecture shaped goals
Lays out a specific career path
Ends by returning to the opening image
why_it_works: A personal experience explains why the future goal matters to you.
Naming concrete next steps makes the plan believable.
Returning to the opening image gives a short essay a finished shape.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Written as a friendly letter, the essay shares the writer's sweet tooth with specific ice cream picks and a dislike of cold weather paired with an offer to knit a blanket. It then covers a wide mix of music tastes, dance and instruments, ending with an offer to play requests.
structure: Opens with a casual greeting and a food obsession
Moves through habits, each paired with an offer to share
Covers music and performing interests
Signs off warmly, looking ahead to living together
why_it_works: Offers to do things for a roommate show generosity, not just traits.
Specific favorites beat general adjectives about yourself.
For Harvard's three-item format, pick the three strongest topics here.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: In a letter to a future roommate, the writer explains how to say their name and how learning its meaning changed their view of it, shares a love of hard math problems, and confesses deep loyalty to Bay Area sports teams, with comfort food after losses. It ends by asking about the roommate.
structure: Opens with name pronunciation and its meaning
Shares an academic passion in a relaxed tone
Adds a sports fandom with highs, lows and snacks
Ends by turning the question back to the roommate
why_it_works: Starting with your name is a natural way to share identity.
Mix one academic interest with personal ones for balance.
Ending with a question makes the note feel like a real conversation.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with an eager attempt to explain an economics idea to an uninterested friend. They then lay out a Princeton plan: economics courses that build on a high school interest in trade, a computing certificate, research on how teenagers handle money, and interests beyond the major such as Latin.
structure: Opens with a short, self-aware anecdote showing enthusiasm
Defines the field as a blend of math, politics and psychology
Maps courses, a certificate and a research idea to Princeton
Adds interests outside the major and campus community structures
Closes with a quick, playful callback
why_it_works: A funny moment of over-enthusiasm proves passion better than claiming it.
Tie each Princeton course or professor to an interest you already have.
A non-major interest shows you would actually use the liberal arts breadth.
sample_essays.match_note: Written when this prompt allowed slightly more words.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: After a stage production sparks their interest, the writer describes teaching themselves gender studies through books, films and an online course. They plan to pair it with economics at Princeton, naming courses, a professor's research, an activist group and a book club, so they can combine data with lived experience in advocacy.
structure: Opens with the moment that sparked self-directed learning
States the advocacy goal and the planned major
Lists courses and groups that fit that goal
Explains why economics complements the main field
Sums up the two-field path
why_it_works: Learning on your own before college shows the interest is real.
Explaining why two fields belong together shows how you think.
Name campus resources that serve your stated goal, not random ones.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer starts inside hands-on engineering workshops, from programming a robot to stress-testing materials. They then show how those experiences point to Princeton's research culture: a biomaterials focus with a named professor, a summer coding program, engineering and computing groups, and faculty whose careers they hope to follow.
structure: Opens inside workshops with several quick hands-on activities
Transitions to wanting that kind of research at Princeton
Lays out a materials research plan with specific faculty
Connects coding experience to campus groups
Closes with faculty role models
why_it_works: Starting with things you built proves real exposure to engineering.
A concrete research plan shows you have studied the department.
Make every Princeton detail connect back to something you have done.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer traces years of programming, from a toy robot to a long-running game project, then argues that computing matters in every field and that they want to be on the building side of whatever comes next. They name a graphics module and a computing history course, and end with a playful wish to meet a famous figure in computing.
structure: Opens with a numbers-backed history of coding projects
Makes a broader case for computing across fields
States a personal mission in one short line
Names specific Princeton courses
Ends with a lighthearted, specific wish
why_it_works: Concrete numbers about time spent make a hobby read as serious.
A big-picture claim about the field shows thinking beyond code.
Trim to the current 250-word limit; this sample runs longer.
sample_essays.match_note: Written when this prompt's limit was 350 words.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer recalls telling classmates as a young child about having two dads and being conceived through IVF, then explains how their family taught them that patient personal talks, not demonstrations, are how minds change. They plan to bring that openness and humor to campus to improve the climate for LGBTQ+ students.
structure: Opens with a childhood moment that started family conversations
Explains the family's belief in change through personal talks
Shows how those talks chipped away at stereotypes over time
Looks ahead to how the writer will engage peers on campus
why_it_works: A childhood anecdote can introduce a lifelong value in a few lines.
Describe how you talk with people, since this prompt is about conversations.
Spend most words on your experience, then end with campus plans.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: In three short sections, each led by a brief identity statement, the writer covers an often-mispronounced name and its cultural meaning, growing up with an early diagnosis that made socializing hard and how music and patience helped, and volunteer work where their suggestions were adopted. A short close says what they hope to share with classmates.
structure: Opens with name mispronunciation and what the name means
Second section traces growth after an early diagnosis
Third section shows community volunteering and its results
Brief closing ties the threads to campus life
why_it_works: Separate headed sections let you cover several identities clearly.
Growth over years answers the question about lessons learned.
Expand the ending to say what classmates would learn from you.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer starts with discolored water at a school fountain, explains how bottled water became a waste problem, and recounts how an environmental club pushed for filtration stations, was turned down by the school board, then rallied the school and crowdfunded until the district agreed. It ends with the stations' measurable impact.
structure: Opens with a sensory moment at a fountain
Lays out the problem and the club's goal
Shows a setback with the school board
Describes the grassroots workaround and fundraising
Ends with concrete results on campus
why_it_works: A problem, setback and solution arc shows persistence in action.
Hard numbers make civic impact concrete.
Choose a local issue you actually changed, not a cause in the abstract.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer mentions a weekly songwriting habit and admits they lack the technical production skills that turn songs into finished tracks. They name creative Princeton peers and an electronic music club as the way they would learn them.
structure: Opens with an existing creative habit
Names the specific technical gap
Points to campus people and a club to fill it
why_it_works: A skill that builds on an existing passion feels purposeful.
Naming precise sub-skills shows you know the craft.
One campus detail makes a 50-word answer school-specific.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer picks humor as the skill to sharpen, admitting that most laughs they get now come from poking fun at themselves. They want to learn to use it in a way that brings people closer together.
structure: States the goal in a short opening fragment
Admits an honest limitation with self-deprecating humor
Ends on how the improved skill would help others
why_it_works: A people skill can be as strong an answer as a technical one.
A small, honest admission makes the goal believable.
Closing on the benefit to others gives the skill a purpose.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Instead of full sentences, the writer answers with a short list. It moves from reading and poetry, through quiet daily rituals and time with a parent, to a favorite view and a shared moment with a close friend that they would like to stretch out.
structure: Opens with literary and intellectual pleasures
Moves to small daily rituals and comforts
Adds family and a favorite view
Ends on a single moment with a friend
why_it_works: A list lets you show many sides of yourself in 50 words.
Ordering items from ideas toward people builds to an emotional close.
Small, specific joys feel more personal than big abstract ones.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer names the loss of real dialogue as society's biggest challenge, pointing to peers stuck in rigid positions and arguing that conversations grounded in lived experience are fading. They warn that this feeds hostility and could push society toward sameness under heavy control.
structure: Opens with an observation about peers' rigid debates
Names what is being lost and its effect
Ends with the larger danger if the trend continues
why_it_works: Grounding a big issue in what you see among peers adds credibility.
Escalating from personal to societal fits a lot into 50 words.
Pick a challenge that reveals what you value.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer asks how anyone can define misuse of AI before trying to regulate it, and argues the answer belongs to sociology and ethics as much as computer science. Pointing to a Stanford program, they call for mixed-discipline committees whose standards center people's welfare, not profit.
structure: Opens with a pointed question about defining AI misuse
Argues the problem crosses disciplines
Names a Stanford program as part of the answer
Ends with a values-based standard
why_it_works: Opening with a question frames a familiar topic in a fresh way.
A quick campus reference shows fit without wasting words.
Name the challenge outright; don't leave the reader to infer it.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer gives each summer its own line instead of writing sentences. Compact fragments pack in a national competition and research, teaching coding, building a practical device for a grandparent's farm, making apps, an internship and tutoring math.
structure: Uses one labeled line for each summer
Lists activities in compact fragments
Ends with a catch-all line covering both summers
why_it_works: Fragments and labels let you fit far more into 50 words.
Strong action words carry a list without extra explanation.
One homey detail, like a build for family, keeps it from reading as a resume.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: In three dense sentences, the writer covers research and app projects, fundraising websites for children abroad, business plans, guest talks at a university in Singapore and running a competition. The answer ends on something no resume would list: enjoying street food with family.
structure: Opens with research and app-building work
Adds fundraising, business planning and public speaking
Ends on a relaxed family moment
why_it_works: Group related activities so a long list has a clear order.
A final non-academic detail reminds readers there is a person behind the projects.
Name places and audiences to make each item concrete.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer jokingly picks watching George Washington shop for clothes and explains a love of presidential trivia. They then argue that small everyday choices can reveal how a leader thinks, ending with a playful question about what he would buy.
structure: Opens with a surprising, funny choice of moment
Explains the personal interest behind it
Turns the joke into a point about leadership
Ends on a light question
why_it_works: An unexpected moment stands out among famous battles and speeches.
Humor works when it leads to a real idea.
Link the moment to a bigger theme you care about.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer chooses a private moment over a famous one: their grandfather, a traditional Chinese medicine doctor who treated families unable to afford hospitals, skipping meals and risking his health to do it. They wish they could sit beside him as he wrote poetry before dawn and ask how he stayed so caring.
structure: Introduces the grandfather and his work
Lists his sacrifices for patients
Notes what he taught the writer
Ends with the exact scene the writer would witness
why_it_works: A family moment can answer a history prompt in a personal way.
Concrete sacrifices show character without adjectives.
End with the specific scene and question you would bring.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with a burst of fragments describing what they see on a long Saturday train ride to a weekend science program. They then show two halves of their mind at work: one rethinking how transit routes are planned, the other noticing a small child pleading with a parent for sweets.
structure: Opens with a string of vivid fragments
Reveals the context: a long trip to a science program
Contrasts the analytical and observant sides of the writer
why_it_works: Describing the commute, not the program, gives a fresh angle.
Showing two ways of thinking reveals personality in one sentence.
Let the activities list cover facts; use this space for texture.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes producing a marketing film in rural China and discovering that background noise had ruined the interviews just when a sponsorship depended on it. After long hours of re-editing, they win the sponsorship along with later internships.
structure: Sets the scene: the project and its location
Introduces the problem and what was at stake
Shows the effort to fix it
Ends with the result
why_it_works: A problem, action and result arc fits neatly into 50 words.
Stating the stakes makes the effort meaningful.
Precise numbers show effort better than adjectives.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: In one long sentence of short items, the writer starts with a wildlife sighting, moves through sports, coding and time with a sibling, and ends with a small act of kindness at a hospital. Each item hints at a value instead of naming it.
structure: Opens with a vivid nature moment
Moves through sports, skills and family
Ends with an act of service
why_it_works: Concrete moments let values show without labels.
Ending on care for others leaves a strong final impression.
Mixing serious and playful items gives a fuller picture.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with a probability puzzle about sharks versus falling airplane parts and explains the psychology of why people misjudge risk. They show how that idea reshaped their debating, including undercutting an opponent's alarming statistics by revealing how harmless many of the counted incidents were.
structure: Opens with a counterintuitive probability question
Explains the mental shortcut behind the wrong guess
Connects the idea to the writer's debate strategy
Shows it working in a real round
Ends on a light, satisfying payoff
why_it_works: Starting with a puzzle invites the reader to think along.
Show an idea changing what you do, not just what you know.
One concrete application proves the excitement is real.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: During lockdown, inspired by a friend's experiment, the writer races through an online AI course and grasps that models improve by repeatedly guessing and correcting. They apply it in a research internship on speeding up infant assessments, question how commercial AI priorities differ from social good, and plan further work at Stanford.
structure: Opens with how the interest began during lockdown
Describes intense self-study and a key insight
Applies the skill in a research internship
Raises an ethical concern about where AI is heading
Ends with plans to keep exploring at Stanford
why_it_works: Name the specific insight that hooked you, not just the course you took.
Raising a critique shows thinking beyond technical skill.
Close with a concrete next project to show the interest is still growing.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Written as a late-night email that apologizes for the hour, the note shares the writer's love of the outdoors with an invitation on a trip and a candid heads-up about one of their quirks. It adds a violin habit with an offer to take song requests, then what they will miss at home.
structure: Opens with a casual, time-stamped greeting
Shares outdoor interests and an invitation
Gives a candid heads-up about a quirk
Adds music with an offer to play requests
Ends on home, family and a cheerful sign-off
why_it_works: A real format, like an email, makes the voice feel natural.
Invitations and offers show what kind of roommate you will be.
A note about what you will miss adds warmth and honesty.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer's letter moves through a sweet tooth with specific ice cream picks and a dislike of cold weather paired with an offer to knit the roommate a blanket. It closes with a wide range of music, dance and instruments, plus an offer to play whatever the roommate wants to hear.
structure: Opens with a casual greeting and a favorite food
Pairs each habit with something the writer will share
Covers music and performing interests
Signs off warmly
why_it_works: Concrete favorites, like named shops, make you easy to picture.
Offers to the roommate show generosity instead of claiming it.
Several short topics give a rounded picture without a long story.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer introduces their Muslim identity and commitment to civil liberties, tracing it to seeing migrant workers in the Middle East. They name specific courses, a student union and a dance group they would join, and end with a goal of becoming a U.S. ambassador to the UN.
structure: Opens with identity and the values it shapes
Ties those values to a formative observation
Names specific campus courses and groups
Ends with an ambitious long-term goal
why_it_works: Link your identity to concrete things you will join on campus.
A bold, specific goal makes your contribution easy to picture.
Show impact you have already had; this sample says little about it.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens at family dinners where a grandfather asks the writer's brothers about school and sports but never asks them, while a grandmother treasures the writer's education. That gap fuels their drive and an idea for a children's book about women in STEM, followed by plans for campus groups, panels and wellness work.
structure: Opens with a family dinner scene showing unequal attention
Contrasts it with a grandmother's support
Explains the drive and a project idea
Lists specific ways to contribute on campus
why_it_works: A small scene can reveal a big motivation without explaining it.
Turning a frustration into a project shows initiative.
Specific campus plans show how you will contribute, not just what you value.

sample_essays.title: Why Electrical Engineering?
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer leads with a goal of making places safer through engineering, then explains that repeated break-ins at a family restaurant exposed a failing system. Crediting a cousin in autonomous systems with sparking the interest, they look ahead from fixing the family's setup to security work at much larger scales.
structure: Opens with a one-line thesis naming the goal
Gives the personal problem behind it
Credits a person who sparked the field interest
Scales the goal from family to nation
why_it_works: A thesis up front makes a 100-word answer easy to follow.
A real-life problem explains why the field matters to you.
Widening the goal step by step shows ambition with a plan.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer pairs an image of the brain and the stars with a months-long search for their own diagnosis at 14. Lucky to have a manageable condition, they turn to children who are not, describing how classes, a neuroscience program and a lecture on care gaps abroad led to a plan for pediatric neurology and humanitarian work.
structure: Opens with a vivid image, then a personal diagnosis
Turns from personal luck to others without access to care
Shows the classes and lecture that defined the problem
Lays out the career path and organizations involved
Ends by returning to the opening image
why_it_works: Name the exact problem you want to solve, not just a field.
Personal experience shows why that problem matters to you.
Cut to fit MIT's 225-word limit; this sample runs a bit longer.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with a run of global issues they follow, links them to an immigrant family background and an international studies focus, then describes classes, self-directed research, a professor to learn from and study abroad. They end by applying the work to local problems like immigration and climate, and to a global career.
structure: Opens with a quick list of issues the writer cares about
Ties the issues to family heritage and school involvement
Shows academic groundwork: classes, research and a professor
Applies the field to local community problems
Ends with long-term career goals
why_it_works: Connect the problems you name to your own background.
Show impact on your local community, which this prompt asks for.
Shorten heavily for MIT; this sample is well over 225 words.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with an injury during a season built around a championship goal and the frustration of watching from the dugout. They then ask to help manage the team, tracking pitch counts and using data to shift the defense and protect the top pitcher. The team falls just short, and the writer reflects on their new role.
structure: Opens with a quick, vivid injury moment
Raises the stakes with the season's goal
Shows the low point of watching from the sidelines
Pivots to a new role with concrete actions
Ends with the result and a clear lesson
why_it_works: Show what you were working toward so the setback costs something.
List the specific things you did to adapt.
Reflect on what you gained, even if the outcome was not a win.
sample_essays.match_note: Written when MIT allowed up to 250 words.

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer sorted their influences under category labels: books and plays, lectures, a memorial site visit, museum and gallery trips, TV, live shows and films. Weighty nonfiction sits beside novels, comedy and thrillers, and no item comes with any explanation.
structure: Groups entries under category labels instead of one long run of titles
Leads with reading that spans politics, economics, social science and fiction
Adds talks, a site visit and exhibits seen in person
Finishes with screen and stage picks across several genres
why_it_works: Labels by type let a reader scan the whole list in seconds.
Mixing serious and fun picks reads as an honest snapshot, not a curated image.
Titles alone are enough; save explanations for prompts that ask for them.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an older version of this prompt that asked for several separate lists (books, publications, films and so on).

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: When the pandemic canceled most summer plans, the writer started two online clubs, one built on talks and reading and one on debate, so classmates stayed in touch. They then explain how that lesson in building connection would shape efforts to support LGBTQ+ students and others at Columbia, naming a specific campus initiative.
structure: Sets up the problem: peers cut off when activities were canceled
Describes the two clubs the writer launched and how each ran
Notes results: weekly highlights, with one club lasting into the school year
Turns to concrete plans for building community at Columbia
why_it_works: Choose a small project you actually ran over a broad statement about identity.
Results, like a club outlasting the summer, prove initiative better than adjectives.
Name the campus program where your skill would carry over, so the plan feels real.

sample_essays.title: Example 3
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer recalls family meals where their schooling got less attention than their siblings', and a relative who prized education they never had. That pushed the writer to write a book for young readers about women scientists. They then list the groups, panels and support spaces they would start or join at Columbia.
structure: Opens on a recurring family meal that reveals an imbalance
Contrasts it with a relative who valued the writer's education
Shows the response: a book for young readers about women scientists
Shifts to specific clubs, events and support spaces planned for Columbia
why_it_works: An everyday household moment can carry as much weight as a dramatic event.
Turning a frustration into a project shows agency rather than complaint.
Offering to found a group signals a builder of community, not just a member.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for Columbia; College Essay Guy doesn't say which prompt, but it answers the same question as this one.

sample_essays.title: Example essay
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer and a parent living in another state disagree about pandemic rules: the parent rejects mask requirements and relies on supplements, while the writer supports public health measures. Invited on their usual yearly trip, the writer goes, but sets clear conditions and personal boundaries that protect both the relationship and their own beliefs.
structure: States the disagreement and both positions plainly
Raises the stakes with an invitation to a family tradition
Shows the writer's choice: go, but on clear conditions
Ends on the boundaries that keep the writer true to their values
why_it_works: Stating your own view plainly makes the way you engaged more meaningful.
Pick a conflict where two things you value pull against each other.
Show the action you took, not just the opinion you hold.

sample_essays.title: Example Essay
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes friendly, recurring debates with a grandparent who has always lived in India, rooted in their very different upbringings, especially over store-bought pain relievers versus traditional remedies. From these talks the writer learned to argue to understand rather than to win, to word disagreement respectfully, and to keep facts apart from hurt feelings.
structure: Introduces the relationship and why their views differ
Zooms in on one recurring argument about medicine
Draws a first lesson about tone and respect
Draws a second about separating logic from emotion
Closes by applying both lessons to future debates
why_it_works: An everyday disagreement can reveal as much as a headline issue.
Give each lesson its own short paragraph so the takeaways are clear.
Show how the conflict brought you closer, not just how it ended.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Volunteering at an exercise camp for students with special needs, the writer finds that one high-energy style fails to reach everyone. Through three students, one who lashes out, one whose goals the writer misread, and one who needs a gentle push, they adjust their approach and conclude that good teaching means recognizing your own limits.
structure: Opens mid-scene with a teaching approach that backfires
Shows the writer adapting for that first student
Repeats the pattern with two more students and new lessons
Ends with a broader lesson about teaching and self-awareness
why_it_works: The obstacle can be your own limits, not an outside disaster.
Pair each moment with what you changed and what you learned.
For 150 words, keep one student's story rather than three.

sample_essays.prompt_answered: Why are you interested in attending Columbia University?
sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer carries questions from a summer seminar on ethics and philosophy into Columbia's Core, names two unusual courses that link chemistry research to wider social questions, points to a summer research program and a sustainability-focused lab, and ends with student dance groups and campus traditions they want to join.
structure: Opens with a one-line thesis naming what draws the writer
Links past seminar questions to the Core and two specific courses
Moves to research: a summer program and one faculty lab
Closes on dance groups and campus traditions
why_it_works: Pair every school detail with something you have already done or asked.
Cover classes, research and student life so the fit feels complete.
Skip location and prestige; pick offerings few other schools have.
sample_essays.match_note: Written when Columbia allowed more words.

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer sets warm memories of trips to a family hometown abroad against the heavy air pollution seen on later visits. They describe summer lab research on a better catalyst for turning a harmful gas byproduct into fuel, then explain why chemistry is how they want to make a difference.
structure: Opens with a quick string of fond travel memories
Turns to the pollution that darkens later visits
Describes summer research aimed at a cleaner chemical process
Ends with a values exercise that confirms the pull toward chemistry
why_it_works: A personal stake explains why a subject matters to you, not just that it interests you.
Use technical terms sparingly so depth shows without losing a general reader.
Close on the goal the field lets you pursue.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an older, longer version of Columbia's areas-of-study prompt.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer traces an interest in physics and space to a goal of building propulsion systems for spacecraft. They map that onto Columbia Engineering: an applied physics major with a mechanical engineering minor, two plasma and nuclear science courses, and research at a campus lab or a partner lab.
structure: Opens with an ambitious career goal tied to space
States the planned major and minor and how they serve the goal
Names two courses and the labs where research could happen
Closes by casting Columbia as the starting point
why_it_works: Under 200 words, lead with the goal and make every detail serve it.
Course numbers and lab names show research in very little space.
Say how each resource moves you toward the goal instead of just listing it.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an older Columbia Engineering "why us" prompt that asks the same thing.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Written as a letter to a coding teacher, the note recalls feeling dismissed and out of place in early coding classes, then credits the teacher with making the field feel welcoming. It names the projects they finished together and the confidence the writer built.
structure: Addresses the teacher directly from the first line
Describes the doubt and isolation of early classes
Marks the turning point when the teacher became an ally
Lists concrete projects finished with the teacher's help
Signs off warmly, as a real note would
why_it_works: Show the before and after so the reader feels what the help changed.
Name shared projects so the thanks is specific, not generic.
A thank-you note can reveal your values without ever stating them.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with tending a flock at a historical site, where climate change first felt real, and recounts environmental clubs, a regional conference and local cleanups they led. Wanting longer-lasting change, they name the Penn environmental group, campus festival and student climate plan they would join.
structure: Opens with an unexpected outdoor image tied to climate awareness
Summarizes a record of environmental leadership and service
Pivots briefly: one-off events are not enough
Names specific Penn groups and projects to join
why_it_works: An unusual opening image earns attention before any list of activities.
A track record makes promises about future involvement believable.
Name real campus groups so your contribution plan sounds concrete.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Taking a cue from friends at Penn who mostly praise how different their classmates are, the writer imagines learning from people unlike themselves: coding with engineers, exploring city restaurants with a food writer, bringing a family-business view to a consulting club, and sharing music at campus events.
structure: Opens with what current students say they value most
Sets up one idea: growing through people unlike yourself
Imagines several specific exchanges across schools and clubs
Ends by casting the writer as someone others could learn from
why_it_works: One clear organizing idea can hold many campus details together.
Show both what you would gain from others and what you would give.
Imagined scenes with named groups feel more real than general excitement.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer frames choosing a college as a science experiment: childhood questions as background, a hypothesis that Penn fits, a clinical internship that sparked an interest in healthcare, then Penn courses, a faculty lab and a related minor as the test, ending with the hypothesis confirmed.
structure: Sets up a scientific-method frame with playful early questions
States the hypothesis that the writer and Penn match
Gives background: a clinical internship tied to a family memory
Tests it with courses, a faculty lab and a minor
Declares the evidence supports the hypothesis
why_it_works: A frame borrowed from your field lets the form itself show your interest.
Make a creative structure organize real content, not just decorate it.
Pair each past experience with the Penn resource that would extend it.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an older Penn prompt that allowed up to 450 words.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer links a love of patterns in math and language to how language can carry history and inequality, describes a summer internship in a language research lab, then turns to applying language skills to economic policy in Latin America through a Wharton concentration, named courses, a regional studies minor and a model diplomacy course.
structure: Opens with a fascination with patterns in math and language
Widens to language as a social barrier, with global examples
Grounds the interest in a summer research internship
Shifts to economic policy and names Wharton's concentration and courses
Adds cross-school plans and closes with a playful self-description
why_it_works: Root a policy issue in an interest you already pursue seriously.
Show what tools the business school adds that your current skills lack.
Reaching into other Penn schools shows you would use the whole university.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an older Penn school-specific prompt that allowed up to 450 words; it targets Wharton.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with dead sea lion pups seen while surfing, describes caring about the planet and about building fixes in equal measure, and plans a materials engineering major with an energy and sustainability minor. Past lab research on corrosion and carbon capture is linked to named Penn faculty, courses and an engineering service group.
structure: Opens with a striking scene of environmental harm near home
Shows two drives at once: protecting nature and building solutions
States major and minor, then links past research to faculty
Names courses and a humanitarian engineering group to join
Returns to the opening image to close
why_it_works: A vivid local scene makes a big issue like climate feel personal.
Connect each lab or course you name to work you have already done.
Include clubs and community, not just academics.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an older Penn prompt with a much longer limit.

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Drawn to diplomacy and the politics of the Middle East, the writer explains how the Open Curriculum lets them pair an international affairs concentration with courses on decision-making, film and the region's history, plus workshops and research through a Brown policy institute. They argue that breadth will make them a better diplomat.
structure: States the core interest and long-term goal up front
Shows the Open Curriculum mixing a concentration with unrelated courses
Narrows to a regional track with specific courses
Adds research centers, then closes on breadth over narrowness
why_it_works: Pair your main interest with surprising side courses to show real exploration.
Name courses and centers so the plan could only be about Brown.
Explain why breadth serves your goal, not just that you like variety.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an older version of Brown's Open Curriculum prompt with the same focus.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Building on a research paper about a 1970s movement that opposed feminism, the writer explains how the Open Curriculum and a gender studies program would let them study the topic through anthropology, history and business. They name specific seminars and courses, and end by admitting uncertainty about the future of the issue.
structure: Opens with an independent research project that sparked the interest
Explains how the Open Curriculum combines several disciplines
Names seminars and courses tied to current issues
Adds an entrepreneurship program for building coalitions
Ends by admitting uncertainty about where the issue is heading
why_it_works: Start from work you have already done to prove the interest is real.
Show one question explored through several disciplines at once.
Admitting what you don't know yet can read as maturity.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an older version of Brown's Open Curriculum prompt.

sample_essays.title: Example 3
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer recalls family meals where their schooling got less attention than their siblings', and a relative who prized education they never had. That pushed the writer to write a book for young readers about women scientists. The essay then lays out groups and events the writer would start at Columbia, the school it was written for.
structure: Opens on a recurring family meal that reveals an imbalance
Contrasts it with a relative who valued the writer's education
Shows the response: a book for young readers about women scientists
Shifts to specific clubs, events and support spaces on campus
why_it_works: Ordinary family moments can fully answer a question about how you grew up.
Show what you did in response, not only how it felt.
When adapting this approach, swap the Columbia plans for specific Brown groups.

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer proposes a course on how modern artists use music in plays, cartoons and films to strengthen visual storytelling, with philosophical readings on music's emotional and physical effects and a final project in which students make their own film or mixed-media work.
structure: Opens by asking where music's influence reaches beyond itself
Defines the course's focus: music in visual storytelling
Adds readings on how music affects people
Ends with a hands-on final project
why_it_works: Design the class concretely: topic, readings and a final assignment.
Pairing an art form with philosophy shows depth beyond being a fan.
A hands-on final project shows you think about how others learn.

sample_essays.title: Bonus example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Starting from a family joke about a parent who banked birthday money, the writer explains how an economist's idea showed that saving, though wise for one person, can hurt the wider economy. Their proposed seminar would explore how people overlook the combined effects of everyday choices, from spending to small environmental habits.
structure: Opens with a light family story about saving money
Introduces an economic idea that overturns the writer's assumption
Proposes a seminar on the hidden group effects of personal choices
Widens the idea to habits like environmental choices
why_it_works: A personal story makes an abstract idea easy to grasp.
Choose an idea that changed your own thinking, so you can teach that shift.
Show the idea's reach by applying it to more than one area of life.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes lying on playground equipment at night with close friends, then stargazing alone and thinking about how old starlight is compared with human history and the books and ideas they love. Only at the end do they name stargazing as their source of calm and joy.
structure: Opens with an image-first scene among close friends at night
Shifts to stargazing alone and thoughts about time
Contrasts the stars' age with human history and ideas
Closes by naming the source of joy outright
why_it_works: Lead with a picture and save the explanation for later.
Let a small pleasure open onto bigger thoughts about what you value.
Holding back the main point keeps a short piece moving.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an earlier, longer version of Brown's joy prompt.

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer admits to being hooked on pickleball after first writing it off, founds a school club when court time runs short, and watches it become one of the largest clubs, pulling in students from many social groups. The joy, they suggest, lies in the friendships the game sparks across those groups.
structure: Opens with a short confession of the obsession
Admits early doubts, then growing skill and enthusiasm
Founds a club that quickly grows
Ends on the community the game creates across groups
why_it_works: Admitting you once dismissed the thing adds honesty and a little humor.
Show action: starting a club turns enjoyment into evidence of initiative.
Let the joy point to something bigger, like bringing different people together.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer names a goal in climate-focused economics, then links specific Dartmouth courses, a campus sustainability group and an energy institute to the campus's renewable energy plans. They round out the picture with a food-focused club and the student humor magazine.
structure: States the career goal in the first line
Names courses and sustainability groups that serve the goal
Moves to life outside class with two student groups
Ends on a playful note about writing humor
why_it_works: In 100 words, state your goal first and build every detail from it.
Picturing yourself on campus in present tense makes fit feel concrete.
Mix academic and social details so the fit covers a whole life.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer links campus trees to a nearby arboretum that first sparked an interest in science, then describes a modified biology major blending disease, environment and history, a course on unequal health outcomes, climate advocacy aimed at Congress, and volunteering with a food nonprofit.
structure: Opens by linking the campus landscape to a childhood place
Traces the interest from science toward social questions
Names a modified major and specific courses
Adds advocacy and volunteering that shaped those interests
why_it_works: A quick sensory link between home and campus makes an efficient opener.
Show how your interests changed over time, not just where they are now.
Dense, specific nouns let 100 words carry a lot.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes family meals where a grandparent asks their older siblings about school but never them, and another grandparent who often speaks of missing out on schooling after immigrating. Spurred by both, the writer writes a book for young readers about women scientists, mentors younger relatives, and grows confident speaking up, closing back at the table where it began.
structure: Opens on a family meal scene that reveals an imbalance
Adds a relative's story that gives the writer motivation
Shows the response: a book for kids and mentoring relatives
Returns to the opening meal scene to show change
why_it_works: Describe your environment through one repeated scene, not a general summary.
Show how others' limits became your motivation, then what you did about it.
Returning to the opening scene at the end makes your change easy to see.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Told as a dated timeline, the essay follows the writer from birth abroad and a family separation caused by immigration, through a new language and climate, a grandparent's death, a new home, a growing love of photography and a youth leadership role, ending with the view that the separation brought more good than hardship.
structure: Uses short, dated entries instead of paragraphs
Opens with birth abroad and a family separation
Moves through adjustment: language, seasons, loss, a new home
Adds new passions and a leadership role
Ends by reframing the early hardship
why_it_works: A creative format can cover years of a life in few words.
Mention a hard event plainly, then let later entries show how you adapted.
Close by reinterpreting your past, not just summarizing it.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for a past Dartmouth prompt; it fits the "introduce yourself" option but needs trimming by about 50 words.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer introduces themselves through small creative habits: inventing words with friends for feelings that lack names, photographing everyday details during lockdown, daily walks with a parent, mixing music and reciting literature, and finally sunrise and sunset photo outings that keep them focused on the moment.
structure: Opens with a quirky habit that shows how the writer thinks
Moves to a lockdown photography project and noticing small things
Adds other passions: music and literature with friends
Ends on photo outings and what the camera teaches them
why_it_works: Introduce yourself through habits and choices rather than adjectives.
Several small, varied details can sketch a personality faster than one big story.
Ending on what a hobby teaches you turns a list into reflection.

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes a fascination with mushrooms: stopping on a city sidewalk to photograph a cluster, a forest trip full of oddly shaped fungi, and curiosity about their many uses. The writer ends by naming qualities of mushrooms they hope to share and saying they will look for them on campus.
structure: Opens with an everyday moment of spotting and photographing mushrooms
Explains what the writer admires about how they grow
Describes a photo collection from a forest trip
Reflects on their uses and the curiosity they spark
Links the mushrooms' qualities to the writer and the campus
why_it_works: An offbeat subject can reveal personality quickly.
Tie the fascination back to qualities you hope to have yourself.
Scenes of noticing show curiosity better than calling yourself curious.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an older Dartmouth prompt with a slightly longer limit; it fits both "What excites you?" and "Celebrate your nerdy side."

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: After repeated break-ins at a family restaurant abroad expose unreliable security devices, the writer sets a goal of building a mobile device that detects and reports intruders. They explain how a combined engineering and psychology path, a course on human behavior, faculty research and a Latinx student group at Dartmouth would help.
structure: Opens with a concrete family problem before naming the topic
States an ambitious invention as the impact goal
Maps the goal to a program, a course and faculty research
Adds community through a student group
Closes by linking the family's hard work to future impact
why_it_works: Root a big impact goal in a problem you have seen up close.
Admit what you still need to learn; it makes an ambitious goal credible.
Show how a second field, like psychology, strengthens your solution.

sample_essays.title: Example 1
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer contrasts the unified picture of the civil rights movement taught in school with a 1963 book about the author's own family conflicts during that era. That reading helps the writer handle their own disagreements with a parent over choosing political candidates, holding a view while respecting the other side.
structure: Opens by questioning a simplified classroom version of history
Summarizes the family conflicts the book describes
Names the insight: resisting injustice can strain close relationships
Connects it to the writer's disagreements with a parent
Closes on a changed assumption about shared experience
why_it_works: Pick a reading that complicates something you were taught, then explain how.
Link the reading to a specific relationship of yours, not a general lesson.
Keep plot summary brief; the reader wants your thinking, not the story.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: After a scene of eagerly explaining an economics idea to an unimpressed friend, the writer explains why economics appeals, ties it to Cornell courses, a possible computer science pairing and an interdisciplinary program, adds language, philosophy, the student paper and club sports, and closes with family ties and campus traditions.
structure: Opens with a lighthearted scene that shows enthusiasm for economics
Explains the appeal and the past research behind the choice
Names courses, a computer science pairing and an interdisciplinary program
Branches into humanities, campus media and sports
Closes with family connections and a playful sign-off
why_it_works: A funny, self-aware opening shows passion without bragging.
Describe past work first so the major reads as a next step.
Spread details across classes and life outside class to show range.

sample_essays.title: Bonus example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Written as a letter to the university, the essay says how the writer first came across Cornell, links their lab experience to a faculty member's stem cell work, and plans minors in economics and linguistics plus Spanish, an a cappella group, and a family-rooted goal of a career joining medicine and research.

Adds minors and language study beyond science
Brings in music and a cappella plans
Ties the threads to a medical goal and a warm sign-off

Combine unexpected interests and show the school supports each one.
End by tying varied threads to a single goal.
sample_essays.match_note: Written for an older Arts and Sciences prompt that focused more on why Cornell.

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Moved by a news story about worldwide poverty, the writer describes local service and a goal of social entrepreneurship. They lay out an applied economics major with a finance focus at Dyson, a food systems elective, leadership and competition plans, service abroad and an inclusion-focused program, and close on overall fit.

Links a summer finance program to the planned major and courses
Adds an elective that fits the poverty and hunger interest
Covers leadership, competitions, service abroad and community
Concludes by restating fit with the school
why_it_works: Open with a problem so later details read as steps toward a solution.
Being honest about what you don't know yet makes ambition believable.
At 650 words, a thesis and clear sections keep a long essay organized.

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer ties an interest in swarm robotics to two named research labs, then picks student engineering teams to join with a design idea for one, reflects on a shared campus workshop, plans teaching and outreach, and connects campus farm work with energy projects, closing with a joke about founding a missing club.
structure: Matches a research interest to specific labs and faculty
Picks student engineering teams and pitches an idea for one
Reflects on a shared workshop and how their view of it changed
Adds mentoring, outreach and farm work that merge two interests

sample_essays.match_note: At about 620 words, it was written for an older, longer Cornell Engineering prompt.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer traces an interest in physics and space to a goal of building propulsion systems for spacecraft, then maps it onto Columbia Engineering: an applied physics major with a mechanical engineering minor, two plasma and nuclear science courses, and research at a campus lab or a partner lab.

States the planned major and minor and how they serve the goal

Closes by casting the school as the starting point
