Course numbers and lab names show research in very little space.
At 193 words, this shows what fits within Cornell's 200-word limit.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: In a few lines, the writer describes a yearly family ritual of building a large holiday display piece by piece, starting in early November with the newest set, adding older ones, and finishing the week before the holiday. They end by saying this ritual is what makes the season feel festive to them.
structure: Opens with when the tradition begins each year
Walks through the build in order, newest pieces first
Ends by naming the feeling the ritual creates
why_it_works: A tiny family ritual is enough for a short joy prompt.
Ordered, concrete steps let the reader picture the scene.
Save the feeling for the last line so it lands.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes lying on playground equipment at night with close friends, then stargazing alone and thinking about how old starlight is compared with human history and the books and ideas they love. Only at the end do they name stargazing as their source of calm and joy.
structure: Opens with an image-first scene among close friends at night
Shifts to stargazing alone and thoughts about time
Contrasts the stars' age with human history and ideas
Closes by naming the source of joy outright
why_it_works: Lead with a picture and save the explanation for later.
Let a small pleasure open onto bigger thoughts about what you value.
At 220 words, this would need halving to fit Cornell's 100-word limit.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer presents Jewish identity and community as central to who they are, honoring relatives lost in the Holocaust through tradition and by sharing survivors' stories. As part of a student leadership group at a Holocaust education center, they took on present-day discrimination and helped build a website telling one survivor's story.
structure: Opens lightly, then names a core identity
Explains the family history behind that commitment
Shows action: a student leadership group and a survivor-story project
Ends with the community the writer hopes to find and build
why_it_works: Lead with the identity or perspective you would actually bring to campus.
Back a value with a concrete project and its result.
For Cornell, add a sentence on how this voice would show up among engineers.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer traces a love of storytelling from a parent's nightly tales to teachers, coaches and peers at school, explains how theatre lets them share emotion and shape their world, and describes performing plays about drugs, alcohol and bullying for younger students, ending with storytelling as a way to help the community.
structure: Opens with a childhood ritual that started the interest
Widens to storytellers met at school and finding theatre
Reflects on what telling stories does for teller and audience
Ends with outreach performances for younger students
why_it_works: Trace an activity back to a personal root to show why it matters.
Move from what you love about it to how it helps other people.
End on one specific use of the activity rather than a general claim.

sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes a school problem: students avoid the tap water and not everyone can afford bottled water. Their environmental student group pushes for filtered water stations, is turned down by the district board, gathers signatures, and crowdfunds the cost until the district agrees. The stations cut plastic waste and turn into a popular gathering spot.
structure: Defines a concrete problem at school
States the club's goal
Shows a setback: the board says no
Describes the petition and crowdfunding that win approval
Ends with measurable results and a social payoff
why_it_works: A problem-to-result story shows impact without boasting.
Include the setback; persistence is what makes the win meaningful.
Close with numbers or visible changes that prove the effort worked.

sample_essays.title: Example 1

They then tie that aim to specific Duke courses, a certificate, a business student society, a social-innovation incubator, and plans to run outreach workshops in Durham schools.

Names courses, a certificate and a workshop that serve that goal
Adds student organizations and an incubator for hands-on practice
Ends with outreach in Durham and a look ahead

Covers classes, campus life and the local city, showing range in a short space.

sample_essays.title: Example 2
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer connects a love of the outdoors to a plan to use robotics for environmental protection. They name a dual-major path, a certificate, several courses and what each would teach, a professor's research, and a student volunteer group that does summer projects abroad.

Outlines a dual major and certificate built around that goal

Ends on how your skills could help others, not only on what Duke offers.

sample_essays.title: Example (written for Colgate)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes how Jewish heritage, and relatives lost in the Holocaust, shaped a commitment to remembrance and education. sample_essays.title: Example 1: Top-of-Mind Identity
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer, raised between two cultures, uses a dorm room filled with objects, food and music from both places to explore a mixed identity. They trace an earlier feeling of belonging nowhere, then reframe that in-between position as a strength they now claim with confidence.

Reframes the mixed identity as an advantage

Bookends with the same question to show change without announcing it.
Grounds feelings in small, concrete scenes rather than general statements about culture.

sample_essays.title: Example 2: No Top-of-Mind Identity
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Without an obvious identity marker to write about, the writer builds the essay around a community centered on telling stories. The thread runs from bedtime stories with a parent to school theater, and finally to a class that performs plays about drugs, alcohol and bullying for younger kids.
structure: Opens by naming the community and a childhood story ritual
Introduces mentors and theater as the next chapter
Explains why storytelling matters to the writer
Ends with performances on tough topics for younger audiences
why_it_works: Shows that an interest-based community can answer an identity prompt as well as a cultural one.
Follows one thread through time, which keeps a short essay unified.
Ends on impact on others, hinting at what the writer would contribute.

sample_essays.title: Option #2 Example Essay (written for Princeton)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer explores frequent debates with a grandfather, focusing on one argument over traditional Eastern remedies versus Western medicine for a headache. The essay shows the writer shifting from trying to win to trading knowledge, and learning to keep reasoning apart from hurt feelings.

Zooms in on one debate, explaining both sides fairly
Shows the shift from winning to sharing and learning
Separates logic from emotion in disagreements
Closes with how the lesson carries into future conversations
why_it_works: Presents the other person's view with respect, which proves the lesson instead of just stating it.
Anchors the essay in one concrete disagreement rather than several vague ones.
Shows a change in the writer's own behavior, not in the other person.

sample_essays.title: Option #3 Example Essay (written for Stanford)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer gets excited about a cognitive bias in which vivid, easy-to-recall examples make risks seem more likely than they are. They show how the idea changed their debate style, swapping dry statistics for a memorable image during a round on environmental activism.

Explains the bias in plain terms
Shows how the idea changed the writer's debate strategy

Ends with a short, funny closing line

Explains a technical concept simply enough for any reader to follow.
A brief, witty final line can land better than a summary.

sample_essays.title: Additional example written for Stanford from Markus
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: After a friend's project sparks interest, the writer teaches themselves the basics of AI, including a fast-paced online course. They then put it to work as a lead intern on research aimed at shortening developmental tests, while asking who the technology actually serves.

Ends with next research steps and campus plans
why_it_works: Shows excitement through what you did next, from coursework to research.
Adds an ethical question, showing thought beyond technical enthusiasm.
Runs over Duke's 250 words, so keep one thread and trim the rest.

sample_essays.title: Example (written for another school)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer recounts starting an art magazine for overlooked student artists with a classmate whose spontaneous, wandering creativity clashed with the writer's slow, methodical approach. As the partner's ideas came together, the writer admits their own way isn't the only right one.

Describes early frustration with the partner's detours
Turns as the partner's ideas form a clear pattern
Shows how combining both styles improved the magazine
Ends by owning the writer's own blind spot
why_it_works: Treats different working styles as a real difference, widening what engaging across differences can mean.
Admits the writer was partly wrong, which makes the growth believable.
Points to concrete results of the collaboration, so the lesson isn't abstract.

sample_essays.title: Example (first Why UChicago sample)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Casting themselves playfully as a thinker about culture, the writer argues UChicago suits their humanities interests. They cite a campus visit to a scholar's archive, digital humanities research, specific courses and a graduate seminar, an interdisciplinary humanities major with a planned capstone, and several clubs.
structure: Opens with a bold self-description and a clear claim of fit
Uses a campus archive visit as the emotional center
Links research, courses and a seminar to the writer's own project
Presents an interdisciplinary major and capstone as the framework
Covers clubs, then circles back to the opening with humor
why_it_works: A personal campus visit gives proof of interest that a list of resources can't.
Organizing resources around one intellectual project keeps a long essay focused.
Light humor suits UChicago and keeps a dense essay readable.

sample_essays.title: Example (third Why UChicago sample)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer opens with an inherited sports fandom, using an unconventional quarterback as a bridge to the school's reputation for independent thinking. A childhood stutter explains their curiosity about the brain, leading to a neuroscience plan, named courses, a research lab, the Core and house life.
structure: Opens with a lighthearted sports analogy for independent thinking
Shares a personal story that explains an academic interest
Names a major, courses and a lab tied to research goals
Adds social plans, then calls back to the opening
why_it_works: A personal origin story makes the academic interest feel earned.
An unexpected analogy can introduce your values with personality.
A callback ending ties a long essay together neatly.

sample_essays.prompt_answered: (2018 Prompt) The popular saying goes, “You are what you eat.” What food has shaped your life or worldview?
sample_essays.title: Example for the 2018 food prompt
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Answering a past food prompt, the writer runs an economics lesson for young children using a bag of lollipops. They try several ways of sharing the candy, each ending unfairly, and conclude that even a tiny economy is hard to run fairly, which drives their interest in real-world problems.
structure: Opens in the middle of a chaotic classroom moment
Introduces the economic idea behind the activity
Tests several ways to share, each failing differently
Shows a child's complaint that keeps the problem open
Reflects on real-world complexity and future study
why_it_works: Turns a playful prompt into serious thinking without losing the fun setup.
Leaves the problem unsolved, which reads as honest curiosity rather than weakness.
Uses a small experiment to show how you think, step by step.

sample_essays.prompt_answered: (2019 Prompt) UChicago has international campus centers around the world, but we don’t have any interplanetary, interstellar, or interdimensional campuses… yet! Propose a spot in time or space, in this or any universe, for a new UChicago campus. What types of courses would be taught at this site? What cultural experiences await students who study there?
sample_essays.title: Example for the 2019 new-campus prompt
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Answering a past prompt about a new campus anywhere in time or space, the writer places it in a universe with an extra spatial dimension. They explain the idea's history, then propose courses, geometry and physics research, and playful details of everyday student life there.

Explains the idea's history and vocabulary simply
Proposes courses and research, one theme per paragraph
Lightens the tone with imagined daily campus life
Ends by picturing the campus as a home for outsiders
why_it_works: Answers every part of the prompt: the place, the courses and student culture.
Shows real math and physics knowledge while staying playful.
One clear theme per paragraph keeps a wild idea easy to follow.

sample_essays.title: Example (written for Fordham)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer ties their faith and international outlook to one formative moment: seeing migrant workers abandoned with few supplies, which sparked their advocacy. They then name a course, a humanitarian student group and a dance group at the target school, and close with a long-term diplomatic goal.
structure: Opens with how the writer sees their own identity
Tells a short origin story behind their advocacy
Names specific courses and groups to join
Ends with an ambitious long-term goal
why_it_works: Moves quickly from background to how you'd engage, which is the prompt's real question.
One vivid moment can explain a value better than a list of activities.
For Northwestern, swap in campus groups and courses that fit your story.

sample_essays.title: Example (written for another school's version of this prompt)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes being the eldest child in a large, low-income family, working summer jobs and living through a stretch of homelessness, then coming out in a conservative religious household. They close by naming campus resources and the everyday ways they'd connect with peers and faculty.
structure: Opens with family size, money pressures and time without housing
Turns to coming out within a religious household
Describes seeking counseling and choosing supportive people
Ends by linking these experiences to campus resources
why_it_works: Shares hard experiences plainly, focusing on what they taught rather than on sympathy.
Shows how background shapes the way you'd engage, which is the prompt's core.
Save more room for the forward-looking part; here it gets only the final paragraph.

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer would paint The Rock as a nighttime scene of a woman's figure trapped behind bars. They explain the image through a classic short story about confinement, connect it to leading a club on sexual assault and to barriers women still face, then name campus groups they'd join.
structure: Opens by describing the painted image in vivid detail
Explains its meaning through a literary reference
Connects the image to the writer's activism and current issues
Closes by naming Northwestern groups that share those values
why_it_works: Describe the image first so the reader can picture it before you explain it.
Use the painting as a doorway to your values and activities.
Ending on campus groups turns a creative prompt into a fit essay.

sample_essays.title: Example (written for a similar Boston College prompt)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer proposes a course questioning human dominance over other species and the planet. A service trip abroad, where the writer witnessed a ceremonial animal slaughter, plus later sustainability work, explains where the idea came from, and the essay closes by laying out the course's central questions.
structure: Opens with a course title and a burst of big questions
Tells the personal experience that sparked the idea
Connects it to later environmental work
Builds an argument about humans and the environment
Ends by listing the questions the course would explore
why_it_works: A personal origin story shows why you, specifically, want this course.
Framing a course around open questions signals real intellectual curiosity.
For Northwestern, cut to 200 words and name ideal classmates or collaborators.

sample_essays.title: Example (one more example with analysis)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: Written as a course description instead of a story, this sample proposes a class on how literature portrays women's bodies, contrasting nurturing-mother images with views of women as productive labor. It applies several critical lenses, then lists a sample lecture, two readings and a guest speaker.
structure: Opens with an interdisciplinary course title and intended students
Summarizes the course's central argument and lenses
Outlines one sample lecture topic
Lists required readings and a guest lecturer
why_it_works: A syllabus format shows academic depth quickly within a tight word count.
Naming which students the course suits hints at the classmates the prompt asks about.
Specific readings and speakers prove you've explored the topic beyond class.

sample_essays.title: Example (written for Northwestern's prompt)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer reflects on being biracial: how people react to their white parent, how they're read differently at home and abroad, and feeling out of place in an Asian student community. They then name Northwestern multicultural programs, a student job and book groups, aiming to mentor other biracial students.
structure: Opens with a direct statement of mixed-race identity
Gives examples of feeling misread or out of place
Names Northwestern programs that offer the missing community
Ends with a goal to mentor other biracial students

Specific offices and programs show real research into the school.
Ending with giving back shows you'd contribute, not just receive.

sample_essays.title: Example (one more example essay)

Growing comfortable with teammates, they eventually raced at a meet. They link this to Northwestern's running club, a reading group, and plans to teach kids about literacy and nutrition.
structure: Opens by clarifying an unexpected role on a team
Admits a weakness: disliking running and feeling slow
Shows growth through the decision to race
Names campus groups and a service plan

Shows the kind of welcoming community you'd seek, not just its name.
Pairing a familiar group with a new interest shows range.

sample_essays.title: Example for Northwestern
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer recalls a first trip to Wrigley Field with family that got rained out, then later family visits to Chicago sights and restaurants. Cubs fandom grows into an interest in baseball statistics and a long research paper on trades, and the essay ties family, city and baseball to Northwestern.

Expands to family traditions around the city
Shows fandom turning into analytical interest
Ties location, family and interest together at the end
why_it_works: A personal history with the city makes interest in the location believable.
Turning a hobby into intellectual work shows growth.
Mention Northwestern before the last line so the link feels central.

sample_essays.title: Example
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer describes handling social media and videos for a volunteer group led by women with chronic illnesses, noting how different their own background is from the members' yet how much they share in goals and humor. Concrete roles, like making videos, show contribution instead of claiming it.
A named campus resource connects past work to future plans.

sample_essays.title: Example (written for another school)
sample_essays.what_the_writer_did: The writer traces a path from coding as a young child, through self-taught languages and teaching at a bootcamp, to deeper study of algorithms and memory systems plus summer projects in protein folding and machine learning. Running servers and building security tools then narrows their focus to privacy and security.
